(p-120) Surah Ibrahim

Makkiyyah in its entirety according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah and Jabir.

Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: except for two verses within it, which are Madaniyyah: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favor of Allah for ingratitude?﴾ and what follows it.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book which We have sent down to you﴾ meaning the Qur'an.

﴿to bring mankind out of darkness into light﴾ On this there are four interpretations. The first: from doubt to certainty.

The second: from innovation (bidʿah) to the Sunnah.

The third: from misguidance to guidance.

The fourth: from disbelief to faith. ﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾ On this there are two interpretations. One of them: by the command of their Lord, as said by al-Dahhak.

(p-121) The second: by the knowledge of their Lord.

﴿to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ Miqsam narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: There was a people who believed in ʿIsa and a people who disbelieved in him. When Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, those who had disbelieved in ʿIsa believed in him, and those who had believed in ʿIsa disbelieved in him, so this verse was revealed.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿who prefer the present life over the Hereafter﴾ On this there are two interpretations. One of them: they choose it over the Hereafter, as said by Abu Malik.

The second: they substitute it for the Hereafter, as mentioned by Ibn ʿIsa. And al-istihbab (preferring, loving) is to expose oneself to loving something.

What they prefer of the present life over the Hereafter may carry two meanings. One: they prefer remaining in the present life over remaining in the Hereafter.

The second: they prefer its bounties over the bounties of the Hereafter.

﴿and bar from the way of Allah﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: from the religion of Allah.

It may also mean: from Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾ On this there are two interpretations. One: they hope in Makkah for a religion other than Islam, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they intend harm (halak) to Muhammad (ﷺ), as said by al-Suddi.

It may also bear a third meaning: that they seek worldly gain by illegitimate means, since the bounty of Allah is not sought except through obedience to Him, not through disobedience.

Al-ʿiwaj with a kasra on the ʿayn (ʿiwaj) refers to religion, matters, land, and everything that is not upright; al-ʿawaj with a fatha on the ʿayn (ʿawaj) refers to everything that is upright, such as a wall or a spear.

(p-122) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We indeed sent Musa with Our signs﴾, that is, with Our proofs and Our evidences. Mujahid said: they are the nine signs. ﴿Bring your people out of darkness into light﴾. This admits of two interpretations:

First: from misguidance to guidance.

Second: from the humiliation of enslavement to the honour of dominion.

﴿And remind them of the Days of Allah﴾. In this there are three interpretations:

First: its meaning is, admonish them with the past days that have gone by for them. This was said by Ibn Jarir.

Second: with the days in which Allah took vengeance upon the earlier generations. This was said by al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd.

Third: that the meaning of the Days of Allah is the blessings of Allah upon them. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b narrated it as a marfu' report.

Blessings are also called "days," and from this is the saying of Amr ibn Kulthum:

"And days for us, bright and long, in which we refused that the kingship should subdue us."

It may also bear a fourth interpretation: that he means the days in which they were enslaved and humiliated, because he warned them before the blessings were bestowed upon them.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one﴾. As-Sabbar (the steadfast, sabbar) is one who is very patient, and ash-Shakur (the grateful, shakur) is one who is very thankful. Qatadah said: he is the servant who, when given, gives thanks, and when tested, is patient.

Al-Sha'bi said: patience is half of faith, and gratitude is half. He recited: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one﴾. And al-Hasan hid from al-Hajjaj for nine years. When news of his death reached him, he said: "O Allah, You have caused him to die, so cause his sunnah to die," and he prostrated in gratitude and recited: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one﴾. He specified the signs for every steadfast, grateful one, though there are signs in it for all people, because it is such a person who takes heed from them, while others are heedless of them.(p-123)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 14, verses 6–8:

His words, mighty and majestic: ﴿And in that is a great trial from your Lord﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. First: it is a blessing from your Lord; this is said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan.

The second: it is the severity of the affliction; this is mentioned by Ibn ʿIsa.

The third: it is a test and an examination; this is said by Ibn Kamil.

His words, mighty and majestic: ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. First: its meaning is "and when your Lord made known," i.e., heard; this is said by al-Dahhak.

The second: "and when your Lord said"; this is said by Abu Malik.

The third: its meaning is "and when your Lord informed you," and from it comes the adhan (call to prayer), because it is an announcement. The poet said:

*Then we did not perceive the light of dawn until we heard the caller (al-adhin) in our gatherings.*

﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. First: "If you are grateful for My bounty, I will surely increase you from My grace"; this is said by al-Rabi.

The second: "If you are grateful for My blessing, I will surely increase you in obedience to Me"; this is said by al-Hasan and Abu Salih.

The third: "If you affirm My oneness and obey Me, I will surely increase you"; this is said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

It may also bear a fourth interpretation: "If you believe, I will surely increase you from the bliss of the Hereafter to the bliss of this world."

Some of the righteous were asked about thanking God, Exalted is He, and he said: "It is that you do not strengthen yourself by His blessings in disobeying Him."

It is related that Dawud (peace be upon him) said: "My Lord, how can I thank You, when my thanking You is itself a renewed blessing from You upon me?" He said: "O Dawud, now you have thanked Me."

﴿But if you deny, indeed My punishment is severe﴾. God, Exalted is He, promised an increase for thanks and punishment for disbelief.(p-124)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 14, verse 9:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And those after them—none knows them but Allah﴾. On this there are two opinions.

The first: that is, after those whom He has mentioned from the earlier nations, there were generations and nations whom He did not relate to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), none knows them but Allah, the Knower of what is in the heavens and the earth.

The second: it refers to the fathers between 'Adnan and Isma'il.

Ibn 'Abbas said: between 'Adnan and Isma'il there are thirty fathers who are not known.

Ibn Mas'ud used to recite: "None knows them but Allah; the genealogists have lied" (kadhaba al-nassabun).

﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, that is, with evidences.

﴿So they put their hands into their mouths﴾. On this there are seven opinions. The first: they bit their fingers out of rage against them. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu 'Ubayda cited the verse of the poet:

"Had Salma seen my emaciation, and the thinness of my bones and hand, and the distance from my family and the harshness of my kin, she would have bitten the tips of her hand out of passion."

The second: when they heard the Book of Allah they marvelled at it and placed their hands over their mouths. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: its meaning is that when their prophet said, "Indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you," they pointed with their fingers to their mouths, meaning "be silent," rejecting him and denying his words. This was said by Abu Salih.

The fourth: its meaning is that they denied them with their mouths. This was said by Mujahid.

The fifth: that they would place their hands over the mouths of the Messengers in rejection of what they said. This was said by al-Hasan.

The sixth: that "the hands" are the blessings, and the meaning is that they returned their blessings with their mouths, denying them.

The seventh: that this is a parable intended to mean that they refrained from accepting the truth and did not believe in the Messengers, just as it is said of one who withholds a reply: "he returned it into his mouth" (radda fi fihi).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 14, verse 10–12:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Their messengers said: "Is there doubt about God?"﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: "Is there doubt about the Oneness of God?" This is what Qatadah said.

The second: "Is there doubt about obedience to God?" It may also bear a third interpretation: "Is there doubt about the power of God?" Because they agree upon it, while they differ about everything else.

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, their Creator, because they had neglected His power.

﴿He calls you that He may forgive you some of your sins﴾: that is, He calls you to repentance so that He may forgive what preceded it of disobedience.

Concerning His words, exalted is He: ﴿from your sins﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: the word "min" (from) is superfluous, and its sense is "that He may forgive you your sins." This is what Abu Ubaydah said.

(p-126) The second: it is not superfluous, and its meaning is that the forgiveness should be in place of your sins, so it came in the manner of a substitute (badal).

﴿And He defers you to a specified term﴾: meaning, until death, so that He will not punish you in this world.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Their messengers said to them: "We are only human beings like you"﴾ admits two interpretations. The first: that their people deny that they should be like them while they are the messengers of God to them.

The second: that their people had asked them for miracles which they had proposed.

Concerning His words, exalted is He: ﴿but God bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ there are three interpretations. The first: with prophethood.

The second: with success (tawfiq) and guidance.

The third: with the recitation of the Qur'an and understanding what is in it. This is what Sahl ibn Abdullah said.

﴿It was not for us to bring you an authority except by the permission of God﴾ regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: with a Book.

The second: with a proof (hujjah).

The third: with a miracle (mu'jizah).

(p-127) "That is for those who fear My standing [before Me]." That is, the standing before Me. He attributed it to Himself because of its being specific to Him. The difference between maqām with a fatḥah and muqām with a ḍammah is that when it is with a ḍammah it is the verbal noun of iqāmah (standing/establishing), and when it is with a fatḥah it is the place of iqāmah (the station).

"And fear My warning." In this there are two opinions: the first is that it is the punishment. The second is that it is the threats contained in the Qur'an.

"And they sought victory." In this there are two opinions: the first is that the messengers sought victory by asking for help, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās. The second is that the disbelievers sought a judgment by calamity, as said by Ibn Zayd.

Regarding "istiftāḥ" there are two opinions: the first is that it means beginning. The second is that it means supplication, as said by al-Kalbī.

"And every obstinate tyrant has failed." Regarding "khāba" there are two opinions: the first is that his deed was lost. The second is that his hope was ruined.

Regarding "jabbār" there are two opinions: the first is that it means the avenger. The second is the arrogant one out of insolence.

Regarding "ʿanīd" there are two opinions. The first is that it means one who opposes the truth. The second is that it means one who keeps far from the truth. The poet said:

"And I am not, when a people's affair is disputed, the first to oppose them obstinately."

"Behind him is Hell." In this there are four opinions. The first: its meaning is that Hell is behind him. Abū ʿUbayda said: "warāʾ" is among the words with opposite meanings, and it applies both to "behind" and "in front" together.

The second: its meaning is that Hell is in front of him, and from this is the poet's saying:

"And behind you is a day you will reach, neither a present one escaping it nor a desert one."

The third: that Hell is hidden and does not appear, so it is "behind" because it is not seen. This is related by Ibn al-Anbārī.

The fourth: "Behind him is Hell" means after his destruction, Hell, as al-Nābigha said:

"I swore, and I left you no doubt, and for a man there is no path behind God."

He meant: there is no path after God.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 14, verse 18:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes upon which the wind blows violently on a stormy day.﴾ This is a parable which Allah the Exalted coined for the deeds of the disbeliever, in that he gains nothing from them. Like ashes, which are the remnant of a fire that has gone, they bring him no benefit. When a violent wind blows upon them, that is, a strong one, it scatters them and he cannot gather them up. Likewise is the disbeliever with his deeds.

Concerning His saying ﴿on a stormy day﴾ there are three opinions. The first: it describes the day with stormy-ness, which is an attribute of the wind, because the wind occurs within it, just as one says "a cold day" or "a hot day," since cold and heat occur within it.

The second: the intended meaning is "on a day of a stormy wind," and the word "wind" has been omitted because it was mentioned before that.

The third: the stormy-ness is an attribute of the wind previously mentioned, but since it came after "day," it follows its i'rab (grammatical case).

﴿They have no power over anything of what they have earned﴾ admits of two meanings. The first: they will have no power in the Hereafter over any of the reward for the righteous deeds they did in this world, since it has been nullified by disbelief. The second: they will have no power over anything of what they acquired of the goods of this world, through the sins they committed, to benefit from it in the Hereafter.

﴿That is the far-straying error.﴾ He made it "far" because what is lost cannot be made up for once death has come.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 14, verses 19–21:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And they will come out before Allah all together﴾, meaning: they will appear before Him, exalted is He, on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then the weak will say to those who were arrogant﴾, and they are the followers.

﴿to those who were arrogant﴾, and they are the leaders who were followed.

﴿Indeed, we were to you followers﴾, meaning: in disbelief, by obeying you.

﴿So will you avail us anything against the punishment of Allah?﴾, meaning: will you repel from us anything? It is said "aghna 'anhu" when one repels harm from him, and "aghnahu" when one delivers benefit to him.

(p-130) ﴿They will say: Had Allah guided us, we would have guided you﴾. In this there are three aspects. The first: had Allah guided us to faith, we would have guided you to it. The second: had Allah guided us to the path of Paradise, we would have guided you to it. The third: had Allah saved us from the punishment, we would have saved you from it.

﴿It is all the same for us whether we show anxiety or endure patiently; for us there is no escape﴾, meaning: no place of deliverance or refuge. It is said that the people of the Fire will say: "O people of the Fire, indeed a people who were anxious and wept in the world were saved, so they [now] become anxious and weep." Then they will say: "O people of the Fire, indeed a people who were patient in the world were saved, so they [now] are patient." At that point they will say: ﴿It is all the same for us whether we show anxiety or endure patiently; for us there is no escape﴾.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 14, verses 22–23:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided﴾, meaning Iblis.

Al-Hasan said: On the Day of Resurrection Iblis will stand in Hell, delivering a sermon from a pulpit of fire, which all creation will hear.

﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth﴾, meaning the Resurrection, Paradise, the Fire, the reward of the obedient and the punishment of the disobedient.

﴿And I promised you﴾, that there would be no Resurrection, no Paradise, no Fire, no reward and no punishment.

﴿But I broke my promise to you. And I did not have over you any authority, except that I invited you and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

(p-131) The first: its meaning is, "I cannot save you, nor can you save me." This is the view of al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The second: its meaning is, "I cannot aid you, nor can you aid me." This is the view of Mujahid.

Al-Musrikh means the one who aids, and al-Sarikh means the one who seeks aid.

The second: "I disbelieved before you in what you associated with me afterward," because Iblis's disbelief preceded theirs.

Regarding the one who greets them with peace there are three views: The first: that Allah Exalted greets them with peace.

The second: that the angels greet them with peace.

The third: that some of them greet others with peace.

(p-132) His words, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Have you not considered how Allah sets forth an example: a good word like a good tree﴾. Regarding "the good word," there are two opinions. The first is that it is faith (al-īmān). This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj.

The second is that it refers to the believer himself. This was said by ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfi and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas.

Regarding "the good tree," there are two opinions. The first is that it is the date palm. ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar and Anas ibn Malik narrated this from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The second is that it is a tree in Paradise. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿Its root is firmly fixed﴾, meaning in the earth.

﴿And its branches are in the sky﴾, meaning reaching toward the sky.

﴿It yields its fruit every season﴾, meaning its produce.

﴿By the permission of its Lord﴾. According to the lexicographers, ḥīn (حِينٌ) means "a period of time."

al-Nābigha said:

Those who cure snakes have feared its deadly venom; it dismisses it at times and takes it back at times.

As for "ḥīn" here, there are six interpretations. The first is that it means every year. This was said by Mujahid, because it bears fruit every year.

The second is every eight months. This was said by ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, because that is the duration of pregnancy, both outwardly and inwardly.

The third is every six months. This was said by al-Ḥasan and ʿIkrima, because that is the duration of pregnancy outwardly.

The fourth is every four months. This was said by Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, because that is the period from its flowering until its harvesting, as they observe it.

(p-133) The fifth is every two months, because that is the period from its ripening until its drying.

The sixth is every morning and evening, because that is the time of its picking. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 14, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: Allah increases them in proofs (adillah) concerning the firm word. The second: Allah keeps them constant (yudimuhum) upon the firm word. From this is the saying of ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawahah:

May Allah keep firm what He has given you of goodness,
as He kept Moses firm, and granted victory as He granted it [to Moses].

Regarding His saying ﴿with the firm word﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: it is the two testimonies (al-shahadatan), and this is the view of Ibn Jarir. The second: it is righteous deeds (al-ʿamal al-salih).

It may also bear a third meaning: that it is the Qur'an.

(p-136) The words of the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favor of Allah for ingratitude?﴾ Regarding them there are five opinions:

First: They are the Quraysh, who exchanged the favor of Allah upon them when He sent His Messenger from among them, by disbelieving in him and rejecting him. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid.

Second: It was revealed concerning the two most wicked men of the Quraysh, the Banu Umayyah and the Banu Makhzum. As for the Banu Umayyah, they were given enjoyment for a time, and as for the Banu Makhzum, they were destroyed on the Day of Badr. This was said by Ali, and something similar is reported from Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Third: They are the leaders of the polytheists on the Day of Badr. This was said by Qatadah.

Fourth: It refers to Jabalah ibn al-Ayham when he was slapped, and Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, granted him retaliation by a similar slap. He was not content, became resentful, apostatized to Christianity, and joined the Romans with a group from his people. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

When he arrived in the land of the Romans, he regretted it and said:

The nobles became Christian out of shame over a slap,
and there was no harm in it had I endured it.
Stubbornness and pride surrounded me because of it,
and the sound eye was struck with the blind one.
Oh, that I were tending camels in my homeland,
and had not denied the words that Umar said.

Fifth: It is general to all the polytheists. This was said by al-Hasan.

The exchanging of the favor of Allah for ingratitude may carry two meanings:
One: They exchanged the favor of Allah upon them in the message by denying the Messenger (ﷺ).
Two: They exchanged the blessings of this world for the punishments of the Hereafter.

﴿And caused their people to settle in the abode of ruin.﴾ Regarding it there are two opinions:

Two: It is the Day of Badr. This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and Mujahid.

I have not seen their like as warrior champions
on the day of battle, when ruin was feared.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 14, verse 31:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Say to My servants who have believed: establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾. In this there are two views. The first: by "secretly" is meant what is hidden, and by "openly" what is apparent, and this is the view of the majority.

The second: "secretly" refers to voluntary charity (tatawwu') and "openly" refers to obligatory charity (fard). This was said by al-Qasim ibn Yahya.

It may also bear a third meaning: "secretly" refers to the charities (sadaqat), and "openly" refers to the expenditures (nafaqat).

﴿Before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor any friendship﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is that there is no ransom and no intercession for the disbeliever.

The second: the meaning of His saying ﴿no trade﴾ is that sins cannot be bought and Paradise cannot be purchased.

The meaning of His saying ﴿nor any friendship﴾ is that there will be no affection among the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, because of their severing of ties.

Then in it there are two views. The first: that khilal is the plural of khullah, like qilal and qullah. The second: that it is a verbal noun (masdar) of khalaltu khilalan, like qatiltu qitalan.

From this is the saying of Labid:

؎ The lightning-flash has become a partner in guidance, a lasting friendship without the friendships (khilal)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 14, verses 32–37:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation﴾. This is the statement of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

His saying ﴿some of my offspring﴾ means Isma'il and his mother Hajar.

﴿In a valley without cultivation﴾ means Makkah, where he settled them in its stony plain (al-Batha'), and there was no one living there, out of trust in Allah and reliance upon Him.

﴿Near Your Sacred House﴾ because it is the qiblah of the prayers, and for this reason he settled them near it.

He attributed the House to Him because no one else possesses it, and he described it as sacred (muharram) because in it is forbidden what is permitted elsewhere, such as sexual intercourse and violation (of its sanctity).

﴿Our Lord, that they may establish prayer﴾ has two possible meanings. The first: he asked Allah, exalted be He, by this that He guide them to establishing the prayer. The second: that he mentioned the reason for their settling there, namely that they might establish prayer.

﴿So make hearts among the people incline toward them﴾. In ﴿hearts (af'idah)﴾ there are two possibilities. The first: al-af'idah is the plural of fu'ad, which means hearts, and the heart is sometimes expressed by fu'ad. The poet said:

"And truly a heart led me in passionate love to you, and it is patient over the long duration of desire."

The second: al-af'idah is the plural of wafd (delegation), so it is as if he said: make delegations of the nations come toward them.

In His saying ﴿incline toward them (tahwi ilayhim)﴾ there are four possible meanings. The first: it means yearn toward them (tahinnu ilayhim). The second: it means descend toward them (tanzilu ilayhim), because Makkah is in a valley, and one who heads to it descends to it. The third: it means ascend toward them (tartafi'u ilayhim), because what is in the hearts, upon its departure from them, is like something elevated above them. The fourth: it means desire them (tahwahum).

It has also been read as tahwa.

Regarding Ibrahim's request that Allah make hearts among the people incline toward them, there are two opinions. The first: that they would desire to dwell in Makkah, so it becomes a sacred city; this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. The second: that they would long for Makkah and make pilgrimage (hajj); this is what Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Had he not said "from the people," the Jews, Christians, Persians and Romans would have made pilgrimage to it.

﴿And provide them with fruits﴾. In this there are two possibilities. The first: he means the fruits of the hearts, by making them beloved to the hearts of people so that they visit them. The second, and it is the apparent meaning: the fruits of palm trees and other trees; so He answered him with the fruits found in al-Ta'if, and what is brought to them from the cities.

﴿That perhaps they may be grateful﴾, i.e., so that they may thank You.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers﴾. Regarding his seeking forgiveness for his parents despite their polytheism, there are three possibilities. The first: they were alive, so he hoped for their faith; therefore he asked forgiveness for them, but when they died in disbelief, he did not seek forgiveness for them. The second: he meant Adam and Eve. The third: he meant his two sons, Isma'il and Is'haq.

Ibrahim used to read: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents﴾, meaning his two sons; and Yahya ibn Ya'mur also read it this way.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 14, verses 38–43:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾. Maymun ibn Mihran said: It is a warning to the wrongdoer and a consolation to the wronged.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Hastening (muhti'in)﴾. There are three interpretations of it.
The first: its meaning is "hurrying" (musri'in). This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and Qatadah. It is derived from ahta'a, yuhti'u, ihta'an, meaning "to hasten." From it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿hastening toward the caller﴾, that is, hurrying.

The poet said:
"Their home is in the Tigris, and indeed I see them in the Tigris, hastening toward the sound."

The second: it means one who gazes continually without blinking. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak.

The third: it means one who lowers his head and does not raise it. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿With heads raised (muqni'i ru'usihim)﴾. The idiom iqna' al-ra's has two interpretations.
One of them: "with heads lowered" in the dialect of Quraysh. This was said by Mu'arrij al-Sadusi and Qatadah.

The second: "with heads raised." Iqna' al-ra's means raising it. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. From it is the saying of the poet:
"He nodded his head toward me and raised it, as if he had seen something that made him covet it."

﴿Their gaze does not return to them﴾, that is, their gaze does not come back to them. The tarf is the glance, and the eye was called tarf because sight occurs through it. Jamil said:
"I lower my gaze away from Juml, out of honor for Juml, and for the gaze that I am unable to match."

﴿And their hearts are empty (hawa')﴾. By al-af'idah (hearts) is meant the places of the hearts, which are the breasts.

As for His saying: ﴿hawa'﴾, there are four interpretations of it.
The first: they move about inside their bodies with no place to settle, so it is as if they are falling. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid.

The second: they have left their places until they reach the throats, so they neither settle nor return. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: they are the bewildered, who understand nothing. This was said by Murrah.

The fourth: they are empty of good, and whatever is empty is hawa'. This was said by Ibn Abbas. From it is the saying of Hassan:
"Unless you convey to Abu Sufyan from me: you are hollow, sapless, empty of wind."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 14, verse 44–46:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And warn mankind of the Day when the punishment will come to them﴾. Its meaning: warn them of the day on which the punishment will come to them, that is, the Day of Resurrection.

He specified it as the day of punishment, although it is also the day of reward, because the speech came in the manner of a threat to the disobedient, even though it includes an encouragement for the obedient.

﴿Then those who did wrong will say: "Our Lord, delay us for a brief term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers."﴾ They asked for a return to the world when the truth had become clear to them in the Hereafter, so that they might make up for the excesses of their sins. But the Hereafter is not an abode of repentance, so that their repentance would be accepted, nor is it an abode of obligation, so that their obligation could be resumed.

God, exalted is He, answered this request, saying: ﴿Did you not swear before, that there would be for you no passing away?﴾ In it there are two interpretations. The first: that there would be for you no transition from this world to the Hereafter; this was said by Mujahid.

The second: that there would be for you no escape from punishment; this was said by al-Hasan.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And they had planned their plan﴾. In it there are two views. The first: that by the plan he meant polytheism; this was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that by it he meant arrogance and tyranny; it concerns the one who acted tyrannically in his kingdom and ascended with the two eagles into the air; this was said by Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

Ibn Abbas also said: it is Nimrod son of Canaan son of Sanhārib son of Ham son of Noah, who built the tower in the town of al-Rass in the region of Kufa, and made its height five thousand cubits and its width three thousand and twenty-five cubits, and ascended from it with the eagles. When he knew that there was no way to the heaven, he took it as a fortress and gathered in it his family and his children so that they might be protected in it. Then Allah struck its building at its foundations, so the tower collapsed upon them and they all perished. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And they had planned their plan﴾.

(p-143) ﴿And with Allah is their plan﴾. In it there are two interpretations. The first: with Allah is their plan, He knowing it and nothing of it hidden from Him; this was said by Ali ibn Isa.

The second: with Allah is their plan, preserved against them until He recompenses them for it; this was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

﴿Though their plan was such that the mountains would be moved by it﴾. In it there are two readings.

The first: with a kasra on the first lam and a fatha on the second, and its meaning is: "Their plan was not such that the mountains would be moved by it," meaning as a belittling of it; this was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan.

The second: with a fatha on the first lam and a damma on the second, and its meaning is: "Though their plan was such that the mountains would be moved by it," meaning as a magnifying of it.

Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Abdullah ibn Abbas and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with them, read: ﴿وإنْ كادَ مَكْرُهم لِتَزُولَ مِنهُ الجِبالُ﴾ [wa-in kāda makruhum litazūla minhu al-jibāl], "though their plan almost moved the mountains from it." Regarding ﴿the mountains﴾ whose removal they meant by their plan, there are two views. The first: the mountains of the earth. The second: Islam and the Qur'an, because of their firmness and steadfastness, like mountains.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 14, verses 47–48:

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿On the Day when the earth will be changed to a different earth﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: it will be replaced by another earth, white like silver, on which no sin has ever been committed. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The earth will be changed into white silver.

The second: it is this same earth, but its form will be changed and its defilement purified. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿And the heavens﴾. Regarding this there are six opinions:

The first: the heavens will be replaced by others, as the earth will be, so the sky will be made of gold and the earth of silver. This was said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

The second: the heavens will be replaced by others, as the earth will be, so the heavens will become gardens (jinan) and the seas will become fires, and the earth will be replaced by another. This was said by Ka'b al-Ahbar.

The third: the change of the heavens is the folding up (takwir) of their suns and the multiplication of their stars. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

The fourth: their change is that they will be rolled up like the folding of the scroll (sijjil) for books. This was said by al-Qasim ibn Yahya.

The fifth: their change is that they will be split open so that they provide no shade. This was said by Ibn Shajara.

The sixth: their change is the variation of their states: they will be in one state like molten metal (al-muhl), in another like a rose, and in another like oil-dregs (al-dihan). This was related by Ibn al-Anbari.

﴿And they will come forth before Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾, meaning they will come to the judgment and command of Allah, exalted is He. al-Hasan narrated, saying: "'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: O Messenger of Allah, on the Day when the earth will be changed to a different earth, where will people be on that day? He said: (This is a matter about which no one has asked me before. Then he said: On the Sirat, O 'A'isha.)"

قَوْلُهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ: ﴿وَتَرى المُجْرِمِينَ يَوْمَئِذٍ مُقَرَّنِينَ في الأصْفادِ﴾ فِيهِ قَوْلانِ: أحَدُهُما: أنَّ الأصْفادَ الأغْلالُ، واحِدُها صَفَدٌ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ حَسّانٍ:

؎ ما بَيْنَ مَأْسُورٍ يُشَدُّ صِفادُهُ صَقْرٍ إذا لاقى الكَرِيهَةَ حامِي

(p-145) الثّانِي: أنَّها القُيُودُ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ عَمْرِو بْنِ كُلْثُومٍ:

؎ فَآبُوا بِالنِّهابِ وبِالسَّبايا ∗∗∗ وأُبْنا بِالمُلُوكِ مُصَفَّدِينا

أيْ مُقَيَّدِينَ.

وَأمّا قَوْلُ النّابِغَةِ الذُّبْيانِيِّ:

؎ هَذا الثَّناءُ فَإنْ تَسْمَعْ لِقائِلِهِ ∗∗∗ فَلَمْ أعْرِضْ، أبَيْتُ اللَّعْنَ، بِالصَّفَدِ

فَأرادَ بِالصَّفَدِ العَطِيَّةَ، وقِيلَ لَها صَفَدٌ لِأنَّها تُقَيِّدُ المَوَدَّةَ.

وَفي المُجْرِمِينَ المُقْرَّنِينَ في الأصْفادِ قَوْلانِ: أحَدُهُما: أنَّهُمُ الكُفّارُ يُجْمَعُونَ في الأصْفادِ كَما اجْتَمَعُوا في الدُّنْيا عَلى المَعاصِي.

الثّانِي: أنَّهُ يَجْمَعُ بَيْنَ الكافِرِ والشَّيْطانِ في الأصْفادِ.

قَوْلُهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ: ﴿سَرابِيلُهم مِن قَطِرانٍ﴾ السَّرابِيلُ: القُمُصُ، واحِدُها سِرْبالٌ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ الأعْشى:

؎ عَهْدِي بِها في الحَيِّ قَدْ سُرْبِلَتْ ∗∗∗ صَفْراءَ مِثْلَ المُهْرَةِ الضّامِرِ

وَفِي القَطِرانِ ها هُنا قَوْلانِ: أحَدُهُما: أنَّهُ القَطِرانُ الَّذِي تَهْنَأُ بِهِ الجِمالُ، قالَهُ الحَسَنُ، وإنَّما جُعِلَتْ سَرابِيلُهم مِن قَطِرانٍ لِإسْراعِ النّارِ إلَيْها.

الثّانِي: أنَّهُ النُّحاسُ الحامِي، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ وسَعِيدُ بْنُ جُبَيْرٍ.

وَقَرَأ عِكْرِمَةُ وسَعِيدُ بْنُ جُبَيْرٍ ﴿مِن قَطِرانٍ﴾ بِكَسْرِ القافِ وتَنْوِينِ الرّاءِ وهَمْزِ آن؛ لِأنَّ القَطْرَ النُّحاسُ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُهُ تَعالى ﴿آتُونِي أُفْرِغْ عَلَيْهِ قِطْرًا﴾ [الكَهْفِ: ٩٦] والآنِي: الحامِي، ومِنهُ قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَبَيْنَ حَمِيمٍ آنٍ﴾ [الرَّحْمَنِ: ٤٤] . (p-146)

؎ They returned with plunder and captives, and we returned with kings shackled (muṣaffadīn)

That is, bound (muqayyadīn).

As for the saying of al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani:

؎ This praise, if you hear its speaker, then I did not turn away, may I not be cursed, from the ṣafad

He meant by ṣafad the gift, and it was said to be ṣafad because it binds affection.

Regarding ﴿the criminals bound together in shackles﴾ there are two views. The first: they are the disbelievers, gathered in the shackles just as they were gathered in this world in acts of disobedience.

The second: it gathers the disbeliever with the Satan in the shackles.

This is the commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 14, verse 52:

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿This is a message (balagh) for mankind﴾ has two interpretations. The first: this warning is sufficient for mankind; this was said by Ibn Shajara. The second: this Qur'an is sufficient for mankind; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

"Those of understanding" (ulu al-albab) means those possessed of intellects (dhawu al-'uqul).

Yaman ibn Ri'ab narrated that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.
